title: AI-Powered Arbitration – Updating Our Terms of Service
summary: General Legal updated its Terms of Service to allow AI-powered arbitration for small-dollar claims, removing the economic incentive behind nuisance…
body_markdown:
One of the best things about this job is the proximity to other people who are thinking critically about how to change the worst parts of the legal industry.


Usually, this enjoyment is academic. Today, it’s also professional.


A few months ago, we got hit with a demand letter from a cookie troll. Without getting too far into the weeds, there are two things worth knowing: (1) we had an industry-standard cookie consent manager in place, and (2) the troll in question does not appear to have held a real job since pleading guilty to and serving time for wire fraud and mail fraud, arising from an “I thought I found a loophole and Amazon would never notice my order-and-return-for-refund scheme” eight years ago.


I raise these two points because, perhaps idealistically, I think the law exists as a general force for good in society. Cookie laws are no exception: they protect real privacy interests. The problem is procedural. When the process around a law evolves such that it is used primarily as a weapon by bad actors — those who acknowledge no actual damages, but know a nominal payout is less friction for us than arbitration (and easier for them than finding a desk job) — then either the law or the process around it needs to change. (Or both!)


In this case, for now, we’re going with a process solution: today we updated our Terms of Service to provide that, for small-dollar claims arising out of our website, either party can elect arbitration via DecisionLayer. DecisionLayer is an AI-powered arbitration service that resolves disputes faster and more affordably, lowering the barrier to having claims heard. When a dispute arises, an AI arbitrator reviews the case and drafts an award, and a human arbitrator gives final review before it issues. Claims are resolved, they say, 30x cheaper and 10x faster than in standard dispute resolution processes.


A few points about how we approached this. The provision is mutual: either side can elect it. It is limited to small-dollar claims, where the cost of the forum most distorts the outcome. And it is meant to be fair as well as efficient: a faster, cheaper process that still ends with a human arbitrator’s review. Our hope is that a forum this accessible changes the settlement math for both sides: a meritorious claimant no longer needs to be bought off to avoid an expensive process, and a defendant no longer needs to pay a nuisance premium simply because defending is costlier than settling.


The cost of litigation shouldn’t be a deterrent to bringing a meritorious claim — but neither should the cost of litigation (or arbitration) be a deterrent to defending one.


To be clear, this is a change to our website terms only. Nothing changes for existing clients under their engagement letters, and nothing changes about how we work with them. But for the next Abmahnanwalt, we’ll see you in (virtual) arbitration.


Key takeaways


- •


General Legal was targeted by a 'cookie troll' demanding payment despite having standard cookie consent measures in place.


- •


The firm updated its Terms of Service to allow either party to elect AI-powered arbitration through DecisionLayer for small-dollar website claims.


- •


DecisionLayer uses AI to draft arbitration awards with human arbitrator final review, resolving disputes 30x cheaper and 10x faster than traditional processes.


- •


The arbitration provision is mutual, limited to small-dollar claims, and designed to remove the economic incentive for nuisance settlements.


- •


This change applies only to website terms, not to existing client engagement letters or attorney-client relationships.


TL;DR


Cookie Troll Demand General Legal received a demand letter despite having industry-standard cookie consent in place


Process Problem Bad actors exploit cookie laws knowing settlement costs less than defense, even without real damages


AI Arbitration Solution Updated Terms of Service allow either party to elect DecisionLayer arbitration for small-dollar claims


How DecisionLayer Works AI drafts arbitration awards with human arbitrator final review, 30x cheaper and 10x faster


Mutual and Fair Either side can elect arbitration; designed to eliminate nuisance settlement incentives


Limited Scope Change applies only to website terms, not client engagement letters or existing relationships


FAQs


### What is a cookie troll?


A cookie troll is someone who sends demand letters claiming cookie consent violations, not to vindicate real privacy harms, but to exploit the fact that paying a small settlement is cheaper for defendants than defending the claim.


### Does this arbitration clause affect existing clients?


No. The arbitration provision applies only to disputes arising from the General Legal website. Nothing changes for existing clients under their engagement letters or how the firm works with them.


### How does DecisionLayer arbitration work?


An AI arbitrator reviews the case and drafts an award, then a human arbitrator conducts final review before the award issues. The process is designed to be 30x cheaper and 10x faster than standard arbitration.


### Can only General Legal elect this arbitration, or can the other party too?


The provision is mutual—either party can elect DecisionLayer arbitration for qualifying small-dollar claims arising from the website.


### Why limit this to small-dollar claims?


Small-dollar claims are where the cost of the dispute resolution forum most distorts outcomes, making it economically rational to settle even meritless claims rather than defend them.
